## Notes on Lamentations 3:45–66

**v. 45:** Calvin says the Hebrew word means sweepings or scrapings, and links it to 1 Cor 4:13, where Paul calls the apostles the world's "offscouring." The word properly means sweepings or scrapings, called by the Greeks περιψήματα. Paul says, that he and his associates were the offscouring (περιψήματα) of the world. He adds that God made Judah's shame public, like an unusual example of his vengeance shown to all nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-45.html
- Gill (Baptist) says God handed them over to the Babylonians to be treated like dirt from the street or dross from metal. He thinks Paul may be alluding to this verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-45.html
- Ellicott (Anglican) notes that "people" is plural in Hebrew and means the heathen nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-45.html
- JFB (Presbyterian) says the apostles were treated this way too, but they rejoiced instead of complaining. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-45.html
- Keil & Delitzsch say the verse points to the scattering of Israel, but mainly to how enemies behaved when Jerusalem fell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-45.htm

**v. 46:** Benson says the enemies "opened their mouths" to mock, scoff at and insult Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-45.html

**vv. 48–51:** Matthew Henry notes that the people continued weeping, they continued waiting; and neither did nor would expect relief and succour from any but the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-45.htm
- Constable says the passage switches from "we" (vv. 41–47) to "I" (vv. 48–66). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-64.html
- Keil & Delitzsch say the prophet speaks in the first person because he had risked his life to keep the people faithful to God, so he feels their misfortune most deeply. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-45.htm

**v. 52:** Matthew Henry links "without cause" to David's enemies, and to the enemies of Christ and his church (John 15:25). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-52.html

**v. 53:** This verse has a real split: is it Jeremiah's own story, or a picture of the nation?
- **About Jeremiah himself:** Barnes (Presbyterian) reads it as an attempt to kill him by throwing him into the cistern and covering the opening with a stone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-53.html Constable points to Jer 38:1–6. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-53.html Coffman (Restoration Movement) says the words describe Jeremiah's imprisonment exactly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-53.html
- **About the people:** Calvin rejects limiting it to Jeremiah, because the prophet undertakes the cause of the whole people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-53.html Matthew Poole takes "dungeon" as a picture of the lowest misery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-53.htm Gill thinks it may describe the captive Jews, who were like dead men in graves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-53.htm
- **Figurative:** The Pulpit Commentary points out that Jeremiah's cistern had "no water, but mire," and nothing records anyone throwing stones at him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-52.html Keil & Delitzsch agree that the details come from images in the Psalms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-53.htm
- **What the stones mean:** Calvin says a stone was laid over the pit, as with Daniel's den, so the pit was like a grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-53.html Keil & Delitzsch say the Hebrew means stones were thrown *at* him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-53.htm
- The Berean Study Bible notes on BibleHub see a hint of Christ's burial and resurrection. https://biblehub.com/lamentations/3-53.htm

**v. 54:** Keil & Delitzsch read "waters over my head" as a figure for distress so deep that life itself is in danger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-53.htm

**v. 55:** Benson compares it to Jonah praying from inside the fish. Even from the lowest dungeon, believers can still reach God (Ps 130:1). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-52.html

**v. 56:** Barnes says God heard by sending Ebedmelech to rescue Jeremiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-57.htm
- Matthew Henry says the Hebrew can be read as thanks ("Thou didst not hide thine ear") or as a request ("hide not"). He sees prayer as the soul's "breathing" toward God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-57.html
- Keil & Delitzsch take the word as "sighing," as Luther and the Vulgate did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-57.htm

**v. 57:** Traditions differ on how God said "Do not fear."
- Calvin (Reformed): this is not a spoken voice. It means God answered the prayer, which is the same as though he raised us up and removed from us every fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-57.html
- Matthew Henry: God said it through the prophets, through his providence, and by grace through the witness of his Spirit with their spirits. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-57.html
- Clarke: any mourner can be told "Fear not" on God's authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-57.html
- Poole: God is present everywhere, but he "draws near" when he shows his goodness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-57.htm
- Gill cites the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase), which says God sent an angel to rescue him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-57.htm
- Guzik: the chapter moves from seeing God as an enemy to finding him as an advocate who says "Do not fear." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/

**v. 58:** Keil & Delitzsch say "my cause" means more than lawsuits. It covers everything that concerns his life and safety. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-57.htm

**v. 59:** Keil & Delitzsch explain "judge my cause" as "help me in my cause." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-64.htm

**vv. 60–62:** Keil & Delitzsch say the speaker appeals to God's knowledge of the enemies' plans. The word for "malice" means thinking about and plotting revenge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-64.htm

**v. 63:** The Pulpit Commentary says "sitting and rising" covers all a person's activities. "I am their music" means he is the subject of their mocking songs (cf. Job 30:9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm

**v. 64:** The biggest disagreement is whether vv. 64–66 are a prayer for vengeance or a prediction.
- **Prediction:** Clarke says these verses are all *declaratory*, not *imprecatory*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-66.html Benson says the verbs are future tense, as the Greek and Latin translations have them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-64.htm
- **Prayer:** Gill thinks they are requests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-64.htm Calvin says the saints who prayed this way were guided by the Holy Spirit and did not indulge their own wishes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-64.html Poole says he asks only for justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-64.htm
- Ellicott notes the words come from Ps 28:4, and Paul repeats them in 2 Tim 4:14. https://biblehub.com/lamentations/3-64.htm

**v. 65:** The Pulpit Commentary prefers "covering of the heart," meaning spiritual blindness like the veil in 2 Cor 3:15, and reads "Thy curse upon them!" as a separate cry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
- Barnes renders it "blindness of heart." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-66.html
- Matthew Henry reads it as "perplexity of heart." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-64.html

**v. 66:** Commentators disagree on how a Christian should read this.
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) defends the prayer. He argues that the Lord's Prayer's "Thy will be done" means the same thing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-66.html
- Chuck Smith says Jesus later taught us to bless those who curse us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-66.html
- The Pulpit Commentary (Spanish edition) says we should not expect Christian gentleness from an old Jewish prophet, and need not defend every request. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-61.html
- Calvin says "under the heavens of the LORD" is emphatic. Softening it weakens the sentence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-66.html
- Guzik quotes Morgan: past rescues gave Jeremiah confidence that God would destroy their enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- A different view: Duncan Heaster (Christadelphian) thinks Jeremiah later regretted this prayer when it came true. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-66.html
